demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
Elena’s world used to be one of order and predictable logic. As a cybersecurity analyst, she spent her days identifying vulnerabilities and building digital fortresses. Her job was to anticipate threats, to see the one flawed line of code in a million, to prevent the breach before it happened. She found a quiet comfort in this control, a sense of purpose that had helped her navigate the silence in her house after her husband, Mateo, passed away from cancer three years ago. Work was her anchor, a place where her meticulous nature was a virtue.

That anchor was ripped away on a rainy Tuesday in November. She was driving home from the office, later than usual, the sky already a bruised purple. The wipers smeared the city lights across her windshield. She was thinking about a complex encryption problem, replaying the logic in her mind. She made a left turn at a familiar intersection, the green arrow glowing reassuringly. She never saw the cyclist until the impact—a sickening thud that felt both muffled and deafeningly loud.

In the disorienting seconds that followed, all she could see was a crumpled bicycle wheel spinning uselessly under a streetlight, like a broken toy. The boy, a teenager, was lying on the wet asphalt. The image is seared into her memory, a permanent afterimage she sees whenever she closes her eyes for too long.

The months since the accident have been a slow-motion collapse. The boy survived, but with injuries the doctors called “life-altering.” The police report cleared her of legal fault—the cyclist had run a red light, no helmet, dark clothing—but the facts provided no relief. In her mind, the logic is simple and brutal: she was behind the wheel, therefore she is the breach. She is the threat she failed to anticipate.

Elena no longer drives. Her car sits in the garage, collecting a fine layer of dust. The thought of getting behind the wheel induces a cold sweat and a tightness in her chest so severe she fears her heart will give out. She now navigates the city through a complicated, time-consuming web of buses and trains, her commute tripling in length. Even as a passenger, she’s not at peace. Every screech of brakes, every sudden lane change from a nearby car, sends a jolt of adrenaline through her. She finds herself mentally tracking every vehicle, her body braced for an impact that never comes.

Her work, once a refuge, has become another source of torment. The concentration required to analyze threat matrices is gone, replaced by a dull hum of anxiety and a looping reel of the accident. A sudden notification sound from a colleague’s computer can make her jump, her heart hammering. She looks at her team, competent and focused, and feels like an imposter. How can she protect a company’s most sensitive assets when she couldn’t protect a boy on a bicycle? The thought runs on a constant, cruel loop: *I am a person who destroys lives.*

Sleep offers little escape. She often wakes up gasping, the image of the spinning wheel fresh in her mind, the phantom sound of the impact echoing in the quiet of her bedroom. She feels a profound detachment from everyone around her. Friends try to reassure her, telling her it wasn’t her fault, but their words are meaningless static. They don’t understand. They can’t see the breach she has become. She exists in a gray, muffled world, convinced that she has forfeited any right to happiness, forever defined by that single, catastrophic moment on a rainy Tuesday evening.
